# The Same 88 Keys — rough draft

In recent years, artificial intelligence has made it possible for anyone to
produce text, images, and video at a professional level. This has led many
people to believe that the tool itself is the source of quality. Therefore, it
is important to consider whether this is actually the case.

The core argument is that tools amplify taste rather than replace it. When
everyone has access to the same model, the same camera, and the same presets,
the output still varies dramatically between individuals. This suggests that the
tool is not the differentiator. The differentiator is the judgment of the person
using it.

We often assume that the barrier to creating good work is technical skill. In
the past, this was largely true. Learning to draw, to write, or to design took
years of practice. However, the new tools have removed that barrier almost
entirely. The first draft is now free.

The result is that the cheap part of the process has become the writing, the
drawing, and the building. The expensive part is knowing what is good. This is a
fundamental shift in where the work happens. Many people are unprepared for this
shift because they were never trained to judge, only to execute.

There are several reasons why this shift is difficult to accept. First, it means
that the tool exposes our limitations rather than hiding them. Second, it means
that improvement requires taste, which is slow to develop. Third, it means that
the tools we celebrate are actually filters for what we already have.

In conclusion, everyone gets the same 88 keys. Some people play Bach and some
people play elevator music, but the piano is identical in both cases. Perhaps
the real question is what the new tools reveal about us. So what do you think?
